To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
14-13 proteins stimulate PKC activity in vitro in a non-specific, dose-dependent manner, and that this stimulation is unrelated to their binding affinity to PKC.

the 14-3-proteins stimulate PKC activity in vitro, but the effect is not related to their affinity for PKC, nor to their 14-3 binding sites, and that the effect is not restricted to PKC-zeta but also occurs with classical PKCs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel aspect of 14-3 proteins, i.e. that they may function as activators of PKC.
the regulation of PKC-z by 14-13 proteins and acidic proteins in general.
the question how 14-3 proteins can act in the signal transduction pathways of PKC and Raf-1.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 14-3 proteins are not involved in the regulation of PKC-z activity.
14-13 proteins do not activate PKC-zeta per se.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

PKC-zeta is a 14-3-binding protein that can be recruited to the plasma membrane by 14-13 proteins, and that this event facilitates coupling of PKC to Raf-1 and subsequent activation of the ERK pathway.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stimulatory effects of 14-3 proteins on PKC activity should not be over-interpreted as a specific effect of the 14-3 binding to PKC.

the stimulatory effect of 14-3 proteins on PKC-zeta and other PKCs is unrelated to the 14-3-zeta interaction, and that the 14-13-zeta interaction may be more relevant for the coupling of PKC to Raf-1 and other proteins than for PKC activity.
14-13 proteins may function as adapters for PKC in the absence of a specific binding site, and that this function may be unrelated to PKC activation.
